title: Who Counted
short: Stand on the quay and find the walls to the west, across the harbour. That harbour was the merchant harbour of the ancient city, and in the year three hundred and five before Christ, with Demetrius's fleet already anchored off the town, the Rhodians counted themselves: about six thousand citizens and as many as a thousand foreigners fit to fight. Then, before the first assault on the walls, they voted what the city would owe the families of the dead. Burial at public expense. A pension for parents and children. Dowries for the daughters. A welfare state written in advance of the casualties. The next track meets you at the wide arch in the sea wall, the Gate of the Virgin. Wait outside it.
long:
Stand on the quay and find the walls to the west, across the harbour. That harbour was the merchant harbour of the ancient city, the open one, where the foreigners' cargo came in; the closed naval harbour with its secret sheds is round the corner to the north. And look south, along the low neck of land that runs toward the next port, Akandia.

In the year three hundred and five before Christ, with the fleet of Demetrius, son of Antigonus, already anchored off the town and his army camped outside the wall, the Rhodian assembly did the thing a city does when it is frightened and well organised: it counted. About six thousand citizens, and as many as a thousand foreigners fit to fight; the foreigners who were no use to the defence were sent out of the city, Diodorus says, to save food and to leave nobody inside with a reason to betray it. Then, before the first assault on the walls, the assembly voted what the city would owe the people its soldiers left behind. Slaves who fought bravely would be bought from their masters, freed, and enrolled as citizens. The fallen would be buried at public expense. Their parents and children would be fed from the public treasury. And, in Diodorus's words, "their unmarried daughters should be given dowries at the public cost", while their sons, on reaching manhood, would be crowned in the theatre at the festival of Dionysus and handed a full suit of armour. Burial, pension, dowry, arms: the four duties of a father, taken over by the state, with the circle drawn wide enough to take in slaves. The rich gave money, the craftsmen gave labour, and Diodorus says they competed to outdo one another. That is a welfare state written in advance of the casualties, and a city paying to marry off its dead men's daughters.

Diodorus calls this the best governed city of the Greeks. It lived on merchants sailing to Egypt, kept friendship with every king and fought in none of their wars, and Alexander had trusted it enough to deposit his will here. When the siege ended, in three hundred and four, the peace said the city was to be autonomous and ungarrisoned and to keep its own revenue, against a hundred hostages. No foreign soldiers, your own taxes, your own laws, and one string attached: Rhodes must side with Antigonus in any war except a war on Ptolemy. That bundle is what sovereignty meant then, and it is worth holding onto all day. Among the first things the Rhodians did with it was say thank you. They built Ptolemy of Egypt a square precinct with colonnades a stade long, a hundred and eighty-five metres or so of covered walk, and, Pausanias says, gave him the name Soter, Saviour, and the name stuck. A small city, handing out names to kings. The third great bill of that war, after the dowries and the precinct, was a statue of their god, and that story begins a few streets in, upstairs in the Knights' hospital.

Now that neck of land to the south. A branch of the ancient city wall ran across it, with two horseshoe towers. After an earthquake in the second century after Christ the Rhodians gave up the old walls, and the abandoned rampart out here was buried under rubbish and slowly became a graveyard; the city went on shrinking for centuries after. So the ground between this harbour and the next is a late Roman cemetery on a rubbish-covered wall, and pushing the dead out to the edge of town is what nearly every regime here has done. The Knights made one exception, for their Grand Masters, who were laid under the floor of a church whose foundations you will pass this morning.

The counting never stopped. In April of eighteen eighty-six an Oxford geographer, Henry Tozer, was rowed ashore at Rhodes by two Turks, two Greeks and a Jew, and called them "a crew that well represented the nationalities which inhabit the place". In twenty twenty-five the port counted five hundred and forty-seven thousand cruise passengers, sixth among the harbours of Greece, and with three million visitors a year in all, the Athens press reached for the verb sinking. You are one of today's count. The harbour is still where this city works out who is here, and what it owes them.

The next track meets you at the wide arch in the sea wall, the Gate of the Virgin. Wait outside it. At the arch you will be handed the four questions the whole day asks.

title: Who Sleeps Inside
short: Stand in front of the arch with the wall running away on both sides of you. The rampart to your left is the one the Knights called the Jews' Wall, because it curved round the Jewish quarter. Every power that has held this town since the Knights kept these walls and rewrote one rule above all: who may sleep inside. So carry four questions with you all day. Who decided. Who paid. Who could own. Who could sleep inside. Today the answer to the last one is a resident's driving permit, or a lease from the Ministry of Culture. Walk through. The roofless church is on your left, and the lane beyond it belongs to the neighbours.
long:
Stand in front of the arch, with the wall on either side of you, and look left, where the rampart runs south along the harbour toward the corner. Before you go through, take four questions with you, because you will be asking them all day: who decided, who paid, who could own, and who could sleep inside these walls. Every power that has held Rhodes since the Knights has kept the walls, and every one of them rewrote the answer to the last question.

Start with the stretch to your left. The Knights of Saint John called it the Jews' Wall, because it curved round the Jewish quarter, and the Jewish quarter begins just inside this gate; you will come back to it before lunch. In fourteen eighty, with the Ottoman guns pounding this south-eastern corner of the town, Grand Master d'Aubusson had the Jews' houses behind the wall pulled down for building stone. The Order's ships also brought home Jewish captives taken at sea, two or three thousand of them, and kept them as slaves to work on these fortifications. The Jewish Virtual Library finishes that story in one flat sentence: in fifteen twenty-two, these captives helped the Turks conquer the fortress. So the stone beside you was partly built by people who slept inside these walls only because they were kept there as slaves, and partly betrayed by them.

Gates here are named by whoever holds the keys. The Knights named theirs mostly for saints; the townspeople named them for where they led. The Italians opened or reopened three in their three decades, one of them the gate the guidebooks say Suleiman rode in through in fifteen twenty-two and then had sealed behind him, though the same guidebooks admit the Knights had bricked it up themselves twenty years before he came. The Italians took the story at its word anyway and reopened it on the four hundredth anniversary of the conquest, which is a sentence in stone if ever there was one. And the one you are standing at was cut by the Greeks, the last power to hold the keys, and named not for a saint or a road but for the ruined church beside it.

And who decides today? The archaeologists keep watch from inside, from an office on the Street of the Knights, and the state's own tourist board insists the place is not a museum but a living, inhabited settlement. It is also a settlement whose biggest landlord is the state. The Ministry of Culture owns some three hundred and sixty-five buildings inside these walls, fifty of them on that one street, and it has started letting them out by tender, the first seven two summers ago. The minister who signed the money for the cables and the squares said the point was to socialise the monuments, whatever that turns out to mean for the people living in them.

How many people sleep inside? Nobody can tell you. The guidebooks say about six thousand; a local travel firm says two and a half thousand; nobody has published a census figure for the walled area. What there is, since April this year, is a permit. A permanent resident may drive in only with a special pass, and there is an app for reporting anyone who cheats. That pass is now the badge of belonging, the way a curfew bell once was. And across the town this year the substitute teachers were being pushed out of their flats before the school year had ended, so that tourists could have them from May to September.

Walk through now. Your next track starts just inside, at the church with no roof on your left. The lane beyond it belongs to the neighbourhood, the oldest institution in the street, which keeps its plastic chairs out and watches who comes in.

title: The Parish and the Lane
short: Stand under the three apses and look at what is left of the side walls, not the sky. This was a church of the Order in the lower town, and it kept its dead close: six burial chapels along one side, seven arched tombs set into the other wall. Up the hill the Knights, who left no children, had the stone do the remembering: here lies, then a name, an office and a date. Now look at the doorsteps as you go. Somewhere along this lane there will be a cat with a notched ear, basil in an olive-oil tin, two plastic chairs. That is the parish's other constitution, the one nobody wrote down: who feeds, who blesses, who sits where. Follow the lanes toward the square with the fountain; the building with the outside staircase was the Knights' courthouse.
long:
Stand where the nave was and look up through the three apses at the sky. Then look at what is left of the side walls. This church was recorded with six burial chapels built against its south side and seven arched tombs set into its north wall. What still stands is the three vaulted apses above you and, the guidebooks say, parts of the chapels. This was not the Greek town's church. The Church of Rhodes says it was the heart of a foundation of the Order, served by the brothers themselves, and in the last hundred years before the siege probably the church of the Latin archbishop. In the southernmost chapel the excavators found forty-five people buried together with a hoard of coins, which they connect to the siege of fifteen twenty-two. The Grand Masters and the brethren of the Convent were buried up the hill in the Order's own church of Saint John.

Something like a hundred of their epitaphs survive, by the archaeologist Anna-Maria Kasdagli's count, and they are remarkably alike. Mostly in Latin, some in French, and nearly every one says the same thing: here lies, then a name, an office and a date. These were men who had sworn never to marry and left no children. In nearly every other household on this island the remembering was done by kin. The Order had to make stone do it instead.

The Greek families who bury their dead in this town today keep a timetable rather than a tombstone. A memorial service on the third day, the ninth and the fortieth, then at three months and six, at one year and at three. For a widow or a daughter that is years in black and a regular walk to the grave with oil for the lamp and a candle, and it ends, as the anthropologist Loring Danforth described, with the bones lifted out of the ground. On Rhodes that happens at six or seven years rather than three, because, as the community president told a local paper in twenty eighteen, the island soil is slow to do its work. The bones are washed, boxed and shelved in the cemetery's ossuary, for a small yearly fee, and if nobody keeps paying they go to the common pit.

The dead are not the only thing that comes up from under this town in winter. From Christmas to Epiphany, Greek households say, the goblins come up from underground, where they spend the rest of the year sawing at the tree that holds up the world. On Rhodes, one local study says, they are called kantharoi. You keep them out with a fire that never goes out, a black cross on the door, and a colander on the step, because they must count its holes and cannot say the word three. On the sixth of January the priest comes round with his sprinkler of holy water and they run, crying, in the chant the folklorists wrote down, "Run, let us run, the mad priest is coming with his sprinkler."

Now step back into the lane and read the other constitution, the one nobody wrote down. Find a cat on a step. It became, in twenty twenty-one, the legal responsibility of the municipality, and if one ear has a notch in it, a neighbour took the trouble: telephoned the town hall to register it, waited for the municipal vet to book a slot, and carried it to the clinic and back; or took it to the free spring campaign that a charity from Hannover has run here since twenty twelve, fifteen thousand cats by twenty twenty-one. An ancient Rhodian would hardly have known a house cat; the Greeks kept weasels for the mice. It is the Ottoman householder, for whom the cat was ritually clean and welcome indoors, who would recognise this lane best.

When you pass basil in an olive-oil tin, that is vasilikos, the royal plant, which Orthodox tradition holds grew where the Empress Helena found the Cross. Sixteen days ago, on the fourteenth of September, it was blessed on a tray under the cross and handed out in church, and the sprig you are looking at may be one of them. Two plastic chairs against a wall are not furniture forgotten outside. They are the household's seat on the neighbourhood, the geitonia, which the anthropologist Renée Hirschon, working in a refugee quarter of Piraeus, found to be a social unit in its own right, with the street rather than the house as the women's arena. And any washing strung across the lane is one thing on these facades that the town's appearance rules never listed, and nobody seems to police it.

Follow the lanes toward the square with the fountain. The building there with the outside staircase was the Knights' courthouse, and the next track begins in the square.

title: The Bell and the Light
short: From under the Marine Gate, look back into the square. Under the Knights a bell marked hours when nobody was to move between quarters, and anyone out after dark carried a light. In fourteen fifty-three a Jewish couple, Ezra and Rebecca, needed the Grand Master's seal to cross between their two quarters while the bell rang, and to go out at night, lamp in hand, to a bath, a pharmacist or a doctor. Under the Ottomans the filter was the gates. In eighteen eighty-six a visitor wrote that Greek shopkeepers left at sunset: no Christian could sleep inside the walls. Who may sleep inside is the question this town has asked for seven centuries. Now back through the gate to Museum Square.
long:
Before you go through the gate, look back across the square to the building at its far corner, where Aristotelous street leaves it. That is the Castellania, the Order's courthouse, and its stair is the point: it climbs the outside of the front that faces that street, a court built to be seen from the square. At the top of the stair an angel holds two shields, the Order's plain cross and the arms of Grand Master Emery d'Amboise; a Gothic frame nearby carries the date fifteen oh seven. On that same south front three crocodiles serve as rain-spouts.

The Order's registers show who sat in judgment and how they lived. One of its judges for criminal cases, in fourteen fifty-three, was a man with a thoroughly Greek name, Nicholas Gorgostares, doctor of law, who went to the Grand Master meaning to marry the serf woman who had borne his two children, and had her freed and her and those children made Roman citizens. A judge of the Order, marrying a serf, petitioning his family into the town.

In February fifteen ten the Order wrote down its rules for the town. A bigamist was paraded through it facing backwards on a donkey, wearing a paper crown, and then rowed the galleys for two years. The Order's statutes also said that free women, their dependants and serfs could not board a ship without the Master's licence, and the captain who took them answered for it. People were an asset here, and were guarded like one. In May fourteen seventy-six the Genoese trader Tobias Lomelino was stopped trying to sail for Genoa with his wife and daughters, and then, being the man who had farmed the Order's customs, let go.

Then there was the night. By custom anyone in the streets after dark carried a light, and a bell marked hours when nobody was to move between quarters. On the eighth of March fourteen fifty-three a Jewish couple, Ezra and Rebecca, who had gone to the Grand Master to protest a forced loan, won a bull from Jean de Lastic. It freed them from the community tax, fifty florins a year in all, their own share four. And it let them cross between the Upper and Lower Jewish quarters even during the hours of bellringing, and go out at night, lamp in hand, to a bath, a pharmacist or a doctor. Two people, a lamp, and a piece of parchment: that is what freedom of the streets looked like here.

Look up the bazaar street climbing out of the square. The Jews of Rhodes called it Arriva del Kadi, up at the Kadi's, because the Ottoman authorities sat at its upper end, and the Ottoman census of eighteen thirty-one lists, beside this very street, a quarter of forty-three souls named for the kadi, the judge. The Italians abolished the kadi's office on the twenty-ninth of March nineteen thirty. Today's market judge is the municipality's Directorate of the Medieval City and Monuments, with its office up on the Street of the Knights. Its appearance regulation, which the town was asking shopkeepers to obey in twenty fifteen, allows one sign per street, whatever that was meant to mean, neither oversized nor lit, goods racks no wider than seventy centimetres, and bans what it calls touting which internationally defames our tourist product. The man calling you to a table from that doorway is breaking a rule, and a Knight's castellan, a kadi and a municipal clerk would each recognise the idea of one. Three market judges in five centuries, all within a few minutes' walk of one fountain.

Now step under the arch of the Marine Gate and face the harbour. After the Knights left, the gates, this one among them, became the sunset filter. Henry Tozer, the Oxford geographer, who landed here in April eighteen eighty-six, put it in his book: "The gates of the city are closed at night, and no Christians are allowed to remain within the walls, so that the Greeks, who occupy shops there, are obliged to quit the place at sunset." Until about eighteen thirty-five they also had to be out by Friday noon, for fear the town would be retaken while every Muslim was on his knees at prayer. On a Greek island, the Greeks slept outside their own city.

Now turn back through the gate and follow the lane north inside the wall to Museum Square. The long building on your left was the Knights' hospital, and upstairs in it, waiting for you, is the face of a god.

title: Our Lords the Sick, and the Price of a God
short: The long building on the south side of this square is the Knights' Hospital, now the museum. Upstairs is a marble head of Helios; the ring of holes round his brow once held metal rays. Not the Colossus, but the same face the city stamped on its coins. This is the face they bought. Pliny says the Rhodians sold the siege engines King Demetrius left behind, raised three hundred talents, and gave the job to Chares of Lindos, who took twelve years to cast a god seventy cubits high, about thirty-three metres. Keep that face for the harbour this afternoon. Then turn left up the cobbled street.
long:
The long building filling the south side of this square is the Hospital of the Knights, begun in fourteen forty, finished in fourteen eighty-nine, and now the Archaeological Museum. Go in and up the great stair. The ward at the top is a hall fifty-one metres long, and along its two long walls are small vaulted cubicles set into the thickness of the masonry. Those, it seems, were privies. The beds here were curtained, with clean sheets, and a Czech pilgrim, John of Lobkowitz, here in fourteen ninety-three, noted that beside each one a door opened onto the balcony, with a privy of its own.

Further along the same floor, in the south wing among the Hellenistic sculpture, is a marble head of a young man with wild hair, over life size, a ring of holes drilled round his brow for metal rays. He is Helios, the sun, carved in the later second century before Christ, more than a century younger than the Colossus, from another statue. But he is the same face the city stamped on its coins from its first years onward, sun on one side, rose on the other. Keep that face. You will need it on the harbour this afternoon.

This is where the god gets paid for. Pliny says the Colossus took twelve years and cost three hundred talents, money from selling the siege engines King Demetrius abandoned when he gave up. The sculptor was Chares of Lindos, a Rhodian, pupil of Lysippus, Alexander's court sculptor. It stood seventy cubits, about thirty-three metres, bronze over iron, with stone packed inside to steady it; Pliny says few people could get their arms round its thumb. How they raised it nobody knows. The one surviving account, going under the name of Philo of Byzantium and written centuries after the statue fell, has the workmen burying each finished course in a mound of earth and casting the next on top, and scholars still argue whether that is memory or invention.

What that money meant in human terms is easier. A talent is six thousand drachmas. In the year Rhodes was founded, four hundred and eight before Christ, the Erechtheion building accounts in Athens pay a drachma a day to citizen, resident foreigner and slave alike, a slave named Somenes fluting a column beside his master. At that rate the Colossus is about one million eight hundred thousand days of work, a crew of four hundred for twelve years. That is arithmetic, not evidence, but it tells you what the money mostly bought: twelve years of people.

The Knights ran this building on a different arithmetic. Their Rule has a chapter on how our lords the sick are to be received and served. A sick man is put to bed and fed as if he were a lord, before the brothers eat, and a third of every house's bread and wine goes to the poor in the hospital. The ward rules put doctors on the floor twice a day, one on night duty, a brother from every tongue on the rounds with them, and a scribe checking prescriptions were followed. No cards, no dice, no books but religious ones. The same pilgrim wrote that the sick here ate off silver. Two names survive from before the hall was finished. One account has the Master hiring a Jewish physician, Jacunda Gratiano, in fourteen forty-five, while these walls were going up, after an oath sworn on the Jewish scriptures. And on the twenty-second of December fourteen fourteen a Hungarian slave called Helena, who worked in the Order's infirmary, was freed in recognition of her services to the sick. One institution: a slave woman on the ward, a Jewish doctor, noble knights on rota, and the patient outranking all of them.

Before you leave, find a grave stele carved a little before three hundred and fifty before Christ: a seated woman, her maid opposite holding the jewel box. The inscription, in one English rendering, reads in part: if there is a highest praise in the world befitting a woman, with this died Kalliarista, daughter of Phileratos, for wisdom and virtue; for this reason her husband Damocles set up this stele as a memorial of love. Daughter of, wife of, mistress of. A Greek woman's whole legal world on one slab. Greek law only let a married woman keep her own name in nineteen eighty-three.

When you come out, turn left up the cobbled street. The inns along it were households with no women and no heirs, and they had to write down everything a family does by custom.

title: A Household Without Heirs
short: Look at the doors as you climb. Each inn on this street was the household of a nation: a common table, a chapel, beds for men newly arrived from home. And it was a household like no other, with no women, no children and no heirs, so everything a family does by custom, the Order had to write down. Its Rule told the brothers to sleep clothed, to go out only in twos or threes, and, at table, to let each one eat his bread in silence. The Italians' chapel lived on the income of two windmills, one of them on the harbour mole, where a single mill still stands today. Under the arcade at the top, look left to the school. That is where this household buried its princes.
long:
Look at the doors as you climb. Every one of them opened on a household. The brothers of the Order lived either in the inn of their own nation or in houses of their own, and an inn was less a barracks than a college hall: one nation's common table, its chapel, its beds for men newly arrived from home. In thirteen forty-five there were about four hundred Hospitallers on Rhodes. On the eve of the last siege, in fifteen twenty-two, two hundred and ninety knights and about three hundred sergeants. The ruling caste of an entire island would have fitted into one parish church, and it was a household with no women, no children and no heirs.

That is why it needed a written constitution for the things a family does by custom. The Rule of Raymond du Puy, which the Pope had approved before eleven fifty-three, told each brother to claim nothing beyond bread, water and clothing; to sleep clothed, in linen or wool, never in fur or bright colours; and, at table, in the Rule's own words, let each one eat his bread in silence. A brother found at his death to have kept property of his own was shamed in public, beaten, and set forty days' penance on bread and water. Nobody was born into this family. A knight had to be the son of a knightly house, born in lawful wedlock, with proofs of nobility that grew stricter with every generation; a serving brother needed only to show he was not a serf. The historian Anthony Luttrell adds, a little drily, that many brothers, served by their slaves, lived comfortably here all the same. The town had its own slave market, and the Order's registers name slaves from Bulgaria, Russia and Circassia; Albanians carried off from their country by ship were to be sold, a ruling of fourteen sixty-one says, in Rhodes Town and not elsewhere. When peace talks with the Sultan Bayezid broke down in thirteen ninety-two, it was because the Turks asked for the right to trade slaves here too.

A household this size needs an income, and this one had a country. The Order had answered to the Pope alone since a bull of eleven thirteen, its head elected for life by the professed brethren; but only when it took Rhodes, in thirteen ten, did it gain territory and begin to strike coins, the mark of a sovereign. The first Grand Master here, Foulques de Villaret, put himself on the silver kneeling barefoot before a double cross. Most of the money never came from Rhodes. It came down a pipe from Europe: every priory from Provence to England sent its surplus, the responsions, up this hill. In thirteen twenty-nine that was a hundred and eighty thousand florins a year, and the Venetian Marino Sanudo wondered aloud how a house with that income could not fit out two or three galleys. Nine years earlier it had owed more than half a million florins, mostly to the Pope's Florentine bankers, the Bardi and the Peruzzi.

The inns themselves ran on local money. A document of fourteen oh one records the chapel of Saint Dominic, inside the hospice of the Italian tongue, endowed by the Order's Admiral, Palamedo di Giovanni, with the income of two windmills. One of them stood on the harbour mole, where a single windmill still stands today. And before the Admiral had it, that mill belonged to two women, Eirene Stamatudine and Eirene Archondo. Women are all through the registers of this supposedly closed quarter. Sophia, daughter of John Diastrique, owned a two-storey hospice inside it. In thirteen forty-seven a Hospitaller sister, Margarita of Negroponte, held apartments near the cathedral and an oven she had built to bake bread for the poor. And in fifteen seventeen the Order was still paying a widow who lived inside the castle, Katherina tou Sinademi, one measure of wheat every month for herself and her seven children. A widow on a grain ration is a truer picture of this street than any coat of arms.

You know this arrangement already. Any Dodecanese village that lived through the last century on money posted home from Australia or America was running the Order's economy in miniature: a household on Rhodes kept alive by wages earned somewhere else, and in trouble the moment the pipe closed. Under the arcade at the top, look left to the school. That is where this household buried its princes, and where you will hear what became of their coffins.

title: One Coffin, Two Burials
short: From the top of the street, look left, to the long, low neoclassical school with the clock tower rising behind it. In front of it, behind a railing, are foundation stubs and one standing fragment of wall. That is all that is left of the Order's own church, where it buried the men it had elected. The Knights had no children, so stone did the remembering. Jacques de Milly was laid in a second-hand ancient Greek sarcophagus in fourteen sixty-one; three years later it was reopened for an infant prince of Savoy, son of the Queen of Cyprus, and his epitaph was cut beneath the master's. That coffin is in Paris now. When you are ready, turn right, to the gate between the two horseshoe towers.
long:
From the top of the street, look left, to the long, low neoclassical school up on its terrace, with the clock tower rising behind it. In front of it, below the terrace wall and behind a railing, is a patch of dug-out ground: stubs of foundation, and one broken piece of wall still standing higher than your head. That is all that shows of the church of Saint John of the Collachium, the Order's own church: the church of a monastic state that chose its prince by vote, and buried him here.

Choosing came first. A Grand Master was elected for life by the professed brethren, and in later years by a college drawn from the tongues whose inns you have just walked past. On paper that made him a prince answerable to nobody but the Pope. In practice, the Pope was enough. In thirteen seventeen knights who had had enough of Foulques de Villaret's spending and high-handedness tried to kill him. He fled to Lindos, and the Order elected Maurice of Pagnac in his place. Pope John the Twenty-second refused to recognise Pagnac, pressed Villaret to resign, and by June of thirteen nineteen a third man, Helion de Villeneuve, had the office. One pope, two masters unmade, a third made. Two centuries on, the Order elected Guy de Blanchefort while he was still away in the west, and he died at sea before he could reach the island he had been chosen to rule. The office did not wait for the man; Fabrizio del Carretto was chosen in his place. The laws themselves came from the Chapter General, the assembly of the whole Order, which alone could make the statutes that bound it. A state with no dynasty, and so a state that had to write down what a family does by habit.

These men had no descendants. No family would boil wheat for them on the Saturday of Souls, as Rhodian families still do for their dead; the Order said its masses, and stone did the rest, and the Order was not fussy about whose stone. Cecil Torr, writing in eighteen eighty-seven, says the tombs of Robert de Juilly, who died in the thirteen seventies, and Jacques de Milly, who died in fourteen sixty-one, were ancient Greek sarcophagi. Juilly's white marble coffin was later turned by the Ottomans into the basin of a public fountain, and then acquired by the Musée de Cluny in Paris, where four of the masters' monuments are now. Milly's was opened again three years after him for an infant prince of Savoy, a son of Queen Charlotte of Cyprus, who had lived less than a month; his epitaph was cut beneath the master's. Carretto, the last master to die on Rhodes, lay under a window on this side, the street side, beneath a slab whose Latin called him restorer of the city and for seven years its ruler for the public good, and said that he lay here, fifteen twenty-one. Where the bones themselves went, nobody wrote down.

Torr adds one detail. A vaulted gallery ran from this church across to the Palace, over the top of the street where you are standing, and in it, he says, every knight had to perform gun-drill at least once a week. Prayer on one side, the master's hall on the other, and the covered walk between them for practice with a gun.

The Order left in fifteen twenty-two and the church became the town's great mosque, and in eighteen fifty-six lightning reached gunpowder stored in the cellars of its old bell tower and took the church, and at least two hundred lives, with it; Carretto's tomb was looted in the wreck. Henry Tozer, who came through thirty years later, recorded that the Turkish authorities had not known the powder was there: a garrison sitting on a magazine nobody had inventoried, until lightning found it. The rubble went into a Muslim school, rebuilt in this neoclassical shape about eighteen ninety-eight. It was one of the last Turkish-language schools on the island; the military junta closed it in nineteen seventy-two and renamed it the Thirteenth City Primary School, and by twenty fifteen a human rights report was describing it as bare walls. Look for yourself and see how it has fared since.

Now turn right, to the gate between the two horseshoe towers: the Palace of the Grand Master. Your next track begins in its courtyard.

title: The Priest Who Named the Year
short: You are standing before the two horseshoe towers of the Palace of the Grand Master, on the hill where the sanctuary of the sun god Helios may have stood. His priesthood was the top of a Rhodian priest's career, and the year was named after him. Every decree and contract was dated in the priesthood of so-and-so, and so was every wine jar that left the harbour, stamped with his name and the month. A jar handle dug up in Jerusalem is dated to within a year or two by the priest's name on it. Two hundred and sixty-six of those names survive in clay: sovereignty as a calendar. Then go out through the west gate of the forecourt to the great gate beyond, and look up for a date in Roman numerals.
long:
You are standing in the forecourt of the Palace of the Grand Master, on a small hill at the top of the Knights' quarter. Look at the two horseshoe towers of the gate, and at whatever flag is flying over them; I want to tell you who has sat on this hill. The best current guess, still untested by any excavation, puts the sanctuary of the sun god Helios under your feet; others put it on the acropolis to the west. So why did a trading city choose the sun?

The answer is a poem. In four hundred and sixty-four before Christ Pindar wrote an ode for a Rhodian boxer, Diagoras, which the Rhodians, ancient commentators say, kept in letters of gold in Athena's temple at Lindos. In it Helios is away when the gods divide the earth, and nobody draws a lot for him. He refuses a re-draw and makes Lachesis, the Fate who allots, swear that an island he can see rising from the sea will be his alone. Rhodes is not conquered or colonised; it rises already belonging to one god, by oath. A title deed. The same poem says the sun's sons hurried uphill to be first to sacrifice to newborn Athena and forgot the fire, and that Zeus rained gold on them anyway and Athena gave them every art of handicraft. Diodorus says the rite was still fireless in his day. A city whose founding story says craft was a gift from heaven will one day build the biggest statue in the world.

When Lindos, Ialysos and Kameiros merged into one state in four hundred and eight before Christ, each kept its own gods, so the new state needed one who belonged to all three and to none. Helios was the answer, and his priest became the man the year was named after, appointed, it seems, in turn from each of the three old cities. Every decree and contract was dated in the priesthood of so-and-so. So was every jar of wine that left the harbour, stamped with the priest's name and the month, which is why the list survives in clay: two hundred and sixty-six priests, beginning around three hundred before Christ and running for two and a half centuries. Most of that list was read off more than a hundred and forty thousand broken handles in Alexandria alone. A jar handle dug up in Jerusalem can be dated to within a year or two by the name on it. Six communities on the mainland opposite dated their documents by him. Sovereignty, on Rhodes, was a calendar, exported by the shipload.

Now the statue: the Colossus, the bronze Helios put up after the great siege. Its dedication says the people of Dorian Rhodes raised it when the wave of war was laid to rest, and ends with a line to hear on this hill: for to those who spring from the race of Heracles dominion is a heritage both on land and sea. That is Pindar's oath again, raised thirty-three metres high. The nearest thing to its face is the Helios head you saw in the museum, a century or more younger, wind in the hair, holes drilled for metal rays.

Then watch who sat here. After Arab raids in six hundred and fifty-four and six hundred and seventy-three, the hill was walled as a Byzantine citadel. After twelve hundred and four a local magnate, Leo Gabalas, called himself Caesar and Lord of Rhodes and the Cyclades and struck coins reading Caesar on one face and Servant of the Emperor on the other: sovereignty hedging its bets. Then the Order, for two centuries. In eighteen eighty-one a history of the island by Edouard Biliotti and the Abbé Cottret described three storeys of vaulted storerooms down to the moat, a courtyard pierced with cisterns still holding grain as the Knights had done, and a convict prison of about two hundred and fifty men. The Italians rebuilt it as a holiday house for their king and for Mussolini; look for the large plaque near the entrance that still carries his name. And in December nineteen eighty-eight Andreas Papandreou hosted the European Council here, so a house rebuilt for a king and a dictator ended by seating Europe's heads of government. Who sits on the hill changes; the hill decides nothing and hosts everyone. Look again at that gate.

When you are done, go out through the small gate on the west side of the forecourt to the great gate beyond it, and look up for a date carved in Roman numerals.

title: Receipts on the Wall
short: You are under the arch of the d'Amboise Gate. Step through to the outer side, facing the moat, turn round and look up. An angel holds two shields up there. One is the plain cross of the Order. The other is the arms of Emery d'Amboise, with his name and the Roman numerals for fifteen twelve cut in the marble below, split in two around the angel's robe. On a Rhodes wall a shield is not decoration. It is a receipt, a date-stamp and a claim: this man paid, in this year, under this Order. Nearly four centuries of sultans left the Knights' shields alone, which is why you can still read the receipt. Back to the forecourt now; at noon the iron gate opens and you can walk on top of the walls.
long:
You are under the arch of the d'Amboise Gate. Walk through to the outer side, facing the bridge and the moat, turn round and look up over the arch. An angel holds two shields up there. One is the plain cross of the Order. The other is Emery d'Amboise's own arms, with his name and the Roman numerals for fifteen twelve cut in the marble below them, split in two around the angel's robe. He was Grand Master until fifteen twelve, and the gate was finished in the year he died.

Here is how to read a shield on a Rhodes wall, because it is not decoration. It is a receipt, a date-stamp and a claim of jurisdiction. Henry Tozer, in eighteen eighty-six, wrote down what he saw: the escutcheons over the dwellings or the gateways, denoting either the possessor or the person by whom they were erected, but all of them containing the cross of the Order. The family shield says who paid. The plain straight-armed cross says under whose sovereignty. On the Marine Gate, the twin-towered one you looked at from Hippocrates Square, the set grows to three, with the King of France in the middle. Because the masters' reigns are known, a shield dates a wall the way a reign dates a coin. And notice who is allowed one: a grand master, a king, a pope, a tongue of the Order, now and then one of its great officers. Never a sergeant-at-arms, whose entry requirement was simply not to be a serf.

What each regime did with the last one's marks tells you about the regime. Ettore Rossi, the historian of the fifteen twenty-two siege, says the Turks left the coats of arms, the gateways and the inscriptions almost intact. Nearly four centuries of sultans did not chisel off the Knights' shields; they added wooden balconies, plaques in Arabic script and fountains. The Italians stripped the balconies off the inns in nineteen sixteen and cleared away the Ottoman houses that had grown up against the walls. The Muslim conqueror kept the Christian shields. The Christian coloniser kept them too, and pulled down the Muslim houses that stood in the way of its plan.

Now the older institution under all of this. Local tradition says a dragon's head hung over this gate until the eighteen thirties, the trophy of a knight said to have killed a beast in a marsh under the hill to the west. The knight is a story for another day. Why does a city hang a trophy on its gate at all? The Greeks who lived here first had an institution for it, what scholars call hero cult. Diodorus has one: Phorbas, a Thessalian sent for by Apollo's oracle to clear the island of snakes, and given a hero's honours when he died. That phrase has a shape: a tomb, a sacrifice there every year, sometimes games. Then there was Althaemenes, a prince of Crete. An oracle said he would kill his father, so he fled here and founded the temple of Zeus on Attavyros, the island's highest mountain. His father came looking for him and landed by night with a few men. There was a fight in the dark with the islanders, Althaemenes ran out to help them, and the spear he threw killed his father, whom he did not recognise. When grief had finished him the Rhodians, on an oracle's orders, gave him a hero's honours too. The old commentator on Pindar adds that the temple on the mountain kept bronze bulls that bellowed when disaster was coming: an alarm system in the form of a cult object. That is how a hero gets a job. He clears the land or founds the shrine, he dies, and the city turns his death into an annual obligation it can put in the calendar.

Look at where those heroes came from. Phorbas from Thessaly. Althaemenes from Crete. Danaus, who put in at Lindos on his way from Egypt with his daughters. Nearly every founder in this island's stories arrived from somewhere else; only the Sun's own line, his sons and the grandsons who named the three old cities, were born here. A port wrote its cosmopolitanism into its origins, and the Knights did the same with a trophy over a gate: this is who cleared the land, and this is who holds it now.

The hero still has a job: the island's airport is named Diagoras, after a boxer who won at Olympia two and a half thousand years ago.

Back through the gates to the Palace forecourt. At noon the iron gate opens and you can walk on top of the walls.

title: The Earthquake Ledger
short: You are on top of the wall, with the moat gardens below you on the right. Around two hundred and twenty-six before Christ an earthquake threw down the walls and the Colossus, and Rhodes sent envoys to the kings. Polybius says they spoke so gravely that the donors felt obliged to them for accepting the presents. What was promised is the inventory of a state: oil for the gymnasium, fifty catapults, three thousand talents to raise the statue. They took what came and, obeying an oracle, left the god lying down. The gardens where you come down were the Jewish cemetery until the nineteen thirties; the quarter that buried its dead there is five minutes north, where the next track begins.
long:
You are walking south along the top of the wall, with the moat on your right, planted now as gardens, and beyond it the roofs of the suburbs. This is the chapter of the Colossus that is about money.

Around two hundred and twenty-six before Christ an earthquake threw down the Colossus and most of the walls and dockyards. The Rhodians sent envoys to the cities and kings of the Greek world, and Polybius says the adroit policy of the Rhodians converted this misfortune into an opportunity: they spoke of the disaster so gravely that they were not only overwhelmed with presents but made the donors feel actually obliged for their acceptance of them.

He kept the list. From Syracuse, seventy-five talents of silver for oil in the gymnasium, fifty catapults, and a statue group of the People of Rhodes crowned by the People of Syracuse. From Ptolemy in Egypt, three hundred talents of silver, a million measures of grain, timber for twenty warships, and three thousand talents to raise the Colossus again, with four hundred and fifty builders. Gifts too from Macedon, from the kings of Asia, and from the cities, each according to its means. That is a state, itemised: walls, docks, ships, oil, meat for the gods, citizens recruited with cash. Polybius adds a sour moral for the kings of his own day, who expected thanks for four or five talents.

Then the twist. Ptolemy had promised three thousand talents for the statue, and paid a third of his cash down at once; the statue was never rebuilt. Strabo says only that in accordance with a certain oracle, the people did not raise it again; later tradition says it was Delphi, Strabo does not say. The assembly that had voted a wonder now voted, with a god's permission, to leave it on the ground, and nobody records the money going back. Piety and accounting were one department.

This wall has always sorted people. In eighteen eighty-six Henry Tozer found that it was forbidden to walk on the walls, and any one who stopped for more than a minute to notice an object was hailed by a sentry; to attempt to sketch was dangerous, since after the war with Russia the garrison feared plans of the fortress. Your stroll was an offence in the eighteen seventies. Beyond the moat on the south side Tozer saw an old Turkish cemetery where, he says, the bones of the besiegers who fell in the siege lie; the Italians turned those graveyards into parks.

The gate where you come down, the Gate of Saint John, was La Puerta de la Sivdad to the Jews of the town, the city gate, and their funerals went out through it to the cemetery that began just outside. A caller cried Pasa la misva, the commandment is passing, and people in the street turned their faces away. In the late nineteen thirties the Italian governors cleared that ground for public gardens. Thousands of graves were moved to the Kallithea road, often paid for by relatives who had emigrated; the graves of about eighteen rabbis were moved at the community's cost; the graves nobody could pay for were destroyed, and two cenotaphs stand for them. About a hundred of the finest stones were built into the Palace behind you. The rest, the stones nobody could read, were laid in empty ground in the new cemetery and forgotten, until the restoration of nineteen ninety-seven uncovered them, fifty-eight years later. The oldest found so far, turned up only in twenty twenty-three, is Haim Provencal's, who died in thirteen sixty-three, under the Knights. Notice who paid, both times: kings for the walls, emigrant cousins for the graves. Rhodes is rescued by its neighbours and rebuilt with money from somewhere else, and it still is: dozens of families come back every July for the memorial services, from the cities their grandparents left for.

Down the steps and five minutes north is a quarter that governed itself for four centuries and can be crossed in four minutes, and a synagogue courtyard with a fountain where the priests washed their hands.

title: The Small Jerusalem
short: Kahal Shalom is two streets up from the foot of the wall. Go in through the door on Dosiadou street, into the courtyard, and find the plaque on its east wall, over the spot where a fountain used to be. It was for washing hands: the Kohanim, the priestly families, washed there before raising their hands to bless the room. For four centuries this quarter ran itself, with its own court for marriages, debts and wills, a fund for the sick, a fund for the poor, and a secret fund, the Fundo Secreto, for the poor who would be shamed by being seen to receive. On Fridays brides walked down the wide street that is now the square. Then the museum, the seahorses, and lunch three minutes on.
long:
Kahal Shalom is two streets up from the foot of the wall. Go in through the door on Dosiadou street; the first thing inside is a courtyard. Find the plaque on its east wall, over the place where a fountain once stood. It is dated Kislev, five thousand three hundred and thirty-eight, which is fifteen seventy-seven. The fountain was for washing hands: the Kohanim, the congregation's priestly families, washed there before raising their hands to bless the room. Inside, look down: the floor is black and white pebbles, the craft that floors courtyards across the old town, Turkish and Greek alike. The women's balcony came only in the nineteen thirties; for three and a half centuries before that the women prayed in the side rooms; those rooms are now the museum.

The people who built this were later known as the small Jerusalem, and they had arrived on terms. A nineteen oh six encyclopedia repeats the tradition that the sultan gave the resettled families twenty years free of tax and a house free of expense. Greek-speaking Jews had been here since Roman times, four hundred of them by a twelfth-century traveller's count, until the Knights ordered them converted or expelled twenty years before the Turks came; what was left took on the Spanish rite.

What they made was a corporation of households. Their court, the Bet Din, handled ritual, business, family law, inheritance and crime. Rhodes bent one rule: a married daughter could inherit what the museum's own account calls a nice portion of her father's estate, though the law did not normally let daughters inherit beside brothers. Welfare ran through three funds: Bikur Holim for the sick and the dead, whose plaque of nineteen twenty-four still hangs at number four Vizantiou street; Ozer Dalim for the poor; and the Fundo Secreto, for the poor who would be shamed by being seen to receive. Schools were where the quarter argued with itself: in eighteen eighty-two the French vice-consul, Moses Franco, opened a school teaching Hebrew, Turkish and French, and after five years the rabbis had it shut. The one that won, finished in nineteen oh four with Rothschild money, taught in French and took girls.

A household was several generations under the oldest man. On a Friday the bride's father led her with musicians down the wide street, and at her own door she said, with your permission, I want to go with my husband, kissed the mezuzah on the doorpost, and rice was thrown. Children were named, in the Sephardic way, for living grandparents, and cousins married cousins: fifteen surnames fill two thirds of the graves. A baby wore a pouch of garlic or salt, a gold coin and a blue bead against the evil eye, the eye the Greek church still keeps a prayer against, the bead a Turkish house hangs by the door.

In eighteen forty a Greek boy vanished. The Greek clergy and the European consuls pressed the governor, Yusuf Pasha; eight Jews were arrested, the chief rabbi Jacob Israel among them, one man was given five hundred blows, and the quarter was sealed for twelve days without food or water. Then Constantinople intervened: everyone acquitted that July, the governor dismissed for torture the empire had just forbidden, the sultan's own decree in November calling the charge a calumny.

Days before the deportation of July nineteen forty-four, a Torah scroll believed to have come from Iberia with the exiles went to the mufti, Sheikh Suleyman Kasiloglou, who, the Times of Israel reports, hid it under the pulpit of a mosque; it is in the National Library of Israel now.

When you come out, go to the square. It was La Kaye Ancha, the wide street, where the wedding processions passed; the street's old fountain stood here, and the seahorses are its replacement. The black column in the middle is the memorial: one thousand six hundred and seventy-three people were gathered here and marched to the harbour on the twenty-third of July nineteen forty-four. In June of this year the Rhodes court ruled that seventy-nine heirless houses and shops of the deported belong to the Greek Jewish welfare body; one registry area is called Synagogue Shalom, and some of those houses are around you. Lunch is three minutes away, on a quiet street off the bazaar, and the next track is about who feeds whom. It is Rob's birthday table.
